items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Med Flory lent me an arrangement... Med Flory, Frank Capp. When they make me an offer I can’t refuse... Med Flory plays two choruses... I say some dumb things when I first come out. And we have an arrangement... Med was tired that night.

ctx.x: Yeah, absolutely. Tell me about what possessed you to try to get your Dream Band going? The big band?

That was just a fluke. It was the biggest fluke. I recorded a band in New York in 1956 or something like that and I was sick because it wasn’t good — not to me, it wasn’t good. I used the same rhythm section that was with my little group. I always try to use the guys who travel with me and kill themselves on the road, to give them a good job. If I did a T.V. show, I was steadily using a quartet, three of the guys from the house band, I want my guys on there. I always tried to push them on there. So I put them on…

idea was I was going to hire six different arrangers and pay tribute to six different band leaders, like Duke Ellington, Lionel Hampton, Count Basie, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman and Artie Shaw. And I was going to take something out of each arrangement, like Artie Shaw’s clarinet chorus on “Stardust” just the first 16 bars, and somewhere would sneak it in the arrangement, or part of Ben Webster’s chorus on “Cottontail,” whatever, you know. And I hired the arrangers that I thought would write for those guys. I put…

items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I’ll play straight for Jack Sheldon, Frank Rossolino, Conte Candoli, Med Flory, these are funny minds.

ctx.x: Well I’ve really enjoyed this and I want to close with the last thing you wrote in your book, and it said, “Even though we know that into each life a little rain must fall, all in all I’ve been very fortunate for I’ve been able to laugh all the way to the bandstand.”

Yeah well it’s true. It really is true, Monk. I’ve been fortunate. ‘Cause I looked forward to getting on stage. I’m at my most comfortable when I’m on stage. Because I don’t work, I have fun. I mean I include my audience, that’s why I don’t like playing big concerts. If I play for people playing in a ballroom at least the audience is close, they’re about two feet away from me so I can tell the guy to get a toupee or whatever, I’m going to tell the guy. Lady get your nose fixed, or whatever it is. I become Don…
Well you figured out how to make it all work and I really admire it. And you’ve made some wonderful —
